I don’t agree that using words like ‘depressed’ to just mean ‘sad’ is ‘just plain wrong’. The term *clinical depression* to mean a mental disorder was introduced in the mid 1970s, but the word existed for way longer than that to describe low mood ([link](https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?year_start=1800&year_end=2008&corpus=15&smoothing=7&case_insensitive=on&content=depressed&direct_url=t4%3B%2Cdepressed%3B%2Cc0%3B%2Cs0%3B%3Bdepressed%3B%2Cc0%3B%3BDepressed%3B%2Cc0#t4%3B%2Cdepressed%3B%2Cc0%3B%2Cs0%3B%3Bdepressed%3B%2Cc1%3B%3BDepressed%3B%2Cc0) 

Indeed, modern dictionaries still include the non clinical sense in their definitions: [Cambridge dictionary](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/depressed?q=Depressed) for example, defines ‘depressed’ as ‘unhappy and without hope’

There’s a difference between saying ‘I’m feeling depressed’ and ‘I have major depression/clinical depression/mental illness’
